claim: ChIP-seq identified 4205 peaks for GFP::SMA-3 at the second larval (L2) stage in C. elegans.
source: ChIP sequencing reads identified 4205 peaks for GFP::SMA-3 and 7065 peaks for SMA-9::GFP (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of ChIP-seq peaks identified for GFP::SMA-3 from experimental data.

claim: ChIP-seq identified 7065 peaks for SMA-9::GFP at the second larval (L2) stage in C. elegans.
source: ChIP sequencing reads identified 4205 peaks for GFP::SMA-3 and 7065 peaks for SMA-9::GFP (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of ChIP-seq peaks identified for SMA-9::GFP from experimental data.

claim: The midpoint of the cumulative probability distribution of inter-centroid distances between SMA-3 and SMA-9 ChIP-seq peaks was 788 bp.
source: The midpoint of the cumulative probability distribution of inter-centroid distances was 788 bp; by contrast, a randomization of the positions of SMA-3 and SMA-9 ChIP peaks expanded the midpoint of the cumulative probability distribution of inter-centroid distances to 8211 bp (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific measurement from analysis of ChIP-seq data and references Figure 1a and b showing the cumulative probability distribution.

claim: Randomization of the positions of SMA-3 and SMA-9 ChIP peaks expanded the midpoint of the cumulative probability distribution of inter-centroid distances to 8211 bp.
source: The midpoint of the cumulative probability distribution of inter-centroid distances was 788 bp; by contrast, a randomization of the positions of SMA-3 and SMA-9 ChIP peaks expanded the midpoint of the cumulative probability distribution of inter-centroid distances to 8211 bp (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific measurement from computational randomization analysis and references Figure 1a and b.

claim: 3101 peaks overlap between SMA-3 and SMA-9 ChIP-seq data.
source: From this analysis, a substantial subset (3101 peaks) of the SMA-3 (73.7%) and SMA-9 (43.9%) peaks overlap (Figure 1d).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of overlapping peaks from ChIP-seq analysis and references Figure 1d showing a Venn diagram.

claim: 73.7% of SMA-3 peaks overlap with SMA-9 peaks.
source: From this analysis, a substantial subset (3101 peaks) of the SMA-3 (73.7%) and SMA-9 (43.9%) peaks overlap (Figure 1d).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific percentage calculated from ChIP-seq data analysis and references Figure 1d.

claim: 43.9% of SMA-9 peaks overlap with SMA-3 peaks.
source: From this analysis, a substantial subset (3101 peaks) of the SMA-3 (73.7%) and SMA-9 (43.9%) peaks overlap (Figure 1d).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific percentage calculated from ChIP-seq data analysis and references Figure 1d.

claim: SMA-3 and SMA-9 frequently bind as either subunits in a complex or in close vicinity to each other along the DNA.
source: This analysis demonstrated an increased representation (approaching 45%) of inter-centroid distances of 100 bp or less (Figure 1a and b), smaller than the average peak size for SMA-3 (400 bp) or SMA-9 (250 bp) (Figure 1c), consistent with the interpretation that SMA-3 and SMA-9 frequently bind as either subunits in a complex or in close vicinity to each other along the DNA.
evidence: The manuscript interprets ChIP-seq data showing close proximity of binding sites as evidence for complex formation or close association.

claim: The average peak size for SMA-3 is 400 bp.
source: This analysis demonstrated an increased representation (approaching 45%) of inter-centroid distances of 100 bp or less (Figure 1a and b), smaller than the average peak size for SMA-3 (400 bp) or SMA-9 (250 bp) (Figure 1c), consistent with the interpretation that SMA-3 and SMA-9 frequently bind as either subunits in a complex or in close vicinity to each other along the DNA.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the average peak size for SMA-3 from ChIP-seq data analysis and references Figure 1c.

claim: The average peak size for SMA-9 is 250 bp.
source: This analysis demonstrated an increased representation (approaching 45%) of inter-centroid distances of 100 bp or less (Figure 1a and b), smaller than the average peak size for SMA-3 (400 bp) or SMA-9 (250 bp) (Figure 1c), consistent with the interpretation that SMA-3 and SMA-9 frequently bind as either subunits in a complex or in close vicinity to each other along the DNA.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the average peak size for SMA-9 from ChIP-seq data analysis and references Figure 1c.

claim: RNA-seq identified 1093 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) downregulated in sma-3 mutants using FDR≤0.05.
source: Using a false discovery rate (FDR)≤0.05, we identified 1093 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) downregulated and 774 upregulated DEGs in sma-3 mutants (Figure 2b, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of downregulated DEGs from RNA-seq analysis and references Figure 2b and Supplementary file 2.

claim: RNA-seq identified 774 upregulated DEGs in sma-3 mutants using FDR≤0.05.
source: Using a false discovery rate (FDR)≤0.05, we identified 1093 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) downregulated and 774 upregulated DEGs in sma-3 mutants (Figure 2b, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of upregulated DEGs from RNA-seq analysis and references Figure 2b and Supplementary file 2.

claim: RNA-seq identified 412 downregulated DEGs in sma-9 mutants using FDR≤0.05.
source: In sma-9 mutants, we identified 412 downregulated DEGs and 371 upregulated DEGs (Figure 2d, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of downregulated DEGs from RNA-seq analysis and references Figure 2d and Supplementary file 2.

claim: RNA-seq identified 371 upregulated DEGs in sma-9 mutants using FDR≤0.05.
source: In sma-9 mutants, we identified 412 downregulated DEGs and 371 upregulated DEGs (Figure 2d, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of upregulated DEGs from RNA-seq analysis and references Figure 2d and Supplementary file 2.

claim: BETA analysis identified 367 direct targets for SMA-3.
source: The BETA analysis identified 367 direct targets for SMA-3 and 332 direct targets for SMA-9 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of direct targets identified by BETA software integrating ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: BETA analysis identified 332 direct targets for SMA-9.
source: The BETA analysis identified 367 direct targets for SMA-3 and 332 direct targets for SMA-9 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of direct targets identified by BETA software integrating ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: Every identified direct target of SMA-3 was downregulated in the sma-3 mutant.
source: Every identified direct target of SMA-3 was downregulated in the sma-3 mutant (Figure 2b), indicating that SMA-3/Smad functions primarily as a transcriptional activator.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from RNA-seq data analysis and references Figure 2b.

claim: SMA-3/Smad functions primarily as a transcriptional activator.
source: Every identified direct target of SMA-3 was downregulated in the sma-3 mutant (Figure 2b), indicating that SMA-3/Smad functions primarily as a transcriptional activator.
evidence: The manuscript infers this function from the observation that all direct targets are downregulated in the mutant.

claim: 46% of direct targets of SMA-9 were upregulated in the sma-9 mutant.
source: In contrast, 46% of direct targets of SMA-9 were upregulated and 53% were downregulated in the sma-9 mutant (Figure 2d, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific percentage calculated from RNA-seq data analysis and references Figure 2d and Supplementary file 3.

claim: 53% of direct targets of SMA-9 were downregulated in the sma-9 mutant.
source: In contrast, 46% of direct targets of SMA-9 were upregulated and 53% were downregulated in the sma-9 mutant (Figure 2d, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific percentage calculated from RNA-seq data analysis and references Figure 2d and Supplementary file 3.

claim: SMA-9 acts as either a transcriptional activator or repressor depending on the genomic context.
source: Thus, SMA-9 likely acts as either a transcriptional activator or repressor depending on the genomic context.
evidence: The manuscript infers this dual function from the observation that SMA-9 direct targets show both upregulation and downregulation in mutants.

claim: Luperchio Overlap Analysis (LOA) identified 882 shared DEGs between sma-3 and sma-9 RNA-seq datasets.
source: Rather than relying on individual RNA-seq analyses, in which arbitrary cut-offs for significance may lead to an underestimation of the overlap, we performed Luperchio Overlap Analysis (LOA) on sma-3 and sma-9 RNA-seq datasets to identify 882 shared DEGs (Supplementary file 4, Vora et al., 2022; Luperchio et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of shared DEGs identified by LOA analysis and cites the method.

claim: BETA/LOA analysis identified 129 co-regulated direct target genes.
source: Processing common occupancy sites with the common DEGs through BETA software (Figure 3a), we identified 129 co-regulated direct target genes (i.e. target genes showing differential expression in both sma-3 and sma-9 mutants versus wild-type, and with overlapping SMA-3 and SMA-9 binding peaks nearby (Supplementary file 5)).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of co-regulated direct targets identified by combined BETA/LOA analysis and references Figure 3a and Supplementary file 5.

claim: 114 of the 129 co-regulated direct targets are activated by both SMA-3 and SMA-9.
source: Most (114) of these 129 co-regulated direct targets are activated by both SMA-3 and SMA-9 (Figure 3b), but 15 of them have reversed regulation in sma-9 mutants compared with sma-3 (Figure 3c), suggesting an antagonistic function that we analyze further below.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of co-activated targets and references Figure 3b.

claim: 15 of the 129 co-regulated direct targets have reversed regulation in sma-9 mutants compared with sma-3.
source: Most (114) of these 129 co-regulated direct targets are activated by both SMA-3 and SMA-9 (Figure 3b), but 15 of them have reversed regulation in sma-9 mutants compared with sma-3 (Figure 3c), suggesting an antagonistic function that we analyze further below.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of targets with reversed regulation and references Figure 3c.

claim: For shared activated targets, the loss of SMA-3 caused a greater fold change than the loss of SMA-9.
source: For shared activated targets, the loss of SMA-3 caused a greater fold change than the loss of SMA-9 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this comparison from RNA-seq data analysis and references Supplementary file 2.

claim: BETA/LOA analysis identified 238 SMA-3-exclusive direct targets.
source: Our BETA/LOA analysis next allowed us to deduce SMA-3-exclusive and SMA-9-exclusive direct targets (i.e. target genes directly regulated exclusively by one factor or the other, but not both), revealing 238 SMA-3-exclusive direct targets (Figure 3d) and 279 SMA-9-exclusive direct targets (Figure 3e and f).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of SMA-3-exclusive direct targets and references Figure 3d.

claim: BETA/LOA analysis identified 279 SMA-9-exclusive direct targets.
source: Our BETA/LOA analysis next allowed us to deduce SMA-3-exclusive and SMA-9-exclusive direct targets (i.e. target genes directly regulated exclusively by one factor or the other, but not both), revealing 238 SMA-3-exclusive direct targets (Figure 3d) and 279 SMA-9-exclusive direct targets (Figure 3e and f).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of SMA-9-exclusive direct targets and references Figure 3e and f.

claim: 129 of the 279 SMA-9-exclusive direct targets are activated by SMA-9.
source: About half (129) of the 279 SMA-9-exclusive direct targets are activated by SMA-9 (Figure 3e), whereas the other half (150) appear to be inhibited by SMA-9 (Figure 3f).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of activated SMA-9-exclusive targets and references Figure 3e.

claim: 150 of the 279 SMA-9-exclusive direct targets appear to be inhibited by SMA-9.
source: About half (129) of the 279 SMA-9-exclusive direct targets are activated by SMA-9 (Figure 3e), whereas the other half (150) appear to be inhibited by SMA-9 (Figure 3f).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of inhibited SMA-9-exclusive targets and references Figure 3f.

claim: Less than 25% of all SMA-3 or SMA-9 sites were associated with HOT sites.
source: Less than 25% of all the numerous SMA-3 or SMA-9 sites were associated with HOT sites.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this percentage from analysis of transcription factor binding overlap and references Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Restricting analysis to functional SMA-9 sites identified by BETA reduced HOT site association down to 15%.
source: Restricting our analysis to just functional SMA-9 sites identified by BETA reduced HOT site association down to 15%, although a similar effect was not observed for functional SMA-3 sites identified by BETA.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this percentage from analysis of functional binding sites.

claim: 40% of SMA-9 sites overlapping with SMA-3 sites were associated with HOT sites.
source: SMA-9-exclusive sites showed even lower HOT site association, whereas 40% of SMA-9 sites overlapping with SMA-3 sites (i.e. co-regulated) were associated with HOT sites.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this percentage from analysis of co-regulated binding sites.

claim: The sma-3; sma-9 double mutant showed an intermediate body size phenotype compared to single mutants.
source: Contrary to expectations, the double mutant was neither the same as nor more severe than the single mutants; instead, it showed an intermediate phenotype (Figure 4a).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from body length measurements and references Figure 4a.

claim: SMA-9 may act as both a positive and negative regulator of body size.
source: This result suggests that SMA-9 may act as both a positive and negative regulator of body size, indicating some antagonistic activity towards SMA-3.
evidence: The manuscript infers this dual role from the intermediate phenotype of the double mutant.

claim: For the target gene C54E4.5, expression in the sma-3; sma-9 double mutant is upregulated and indistinguishable from the expression in sma-9 single mutants.
source: In the double mutant, C54E4.5 is upregulated and indistinguishable from the expression in sma-9 single mutants (Figure 4b).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from qRT-PCR analysis and references Figure 4b.

claim: For C54E4.5, the sma-9 loss-of-function phenotype is epistatic to that of sma-3.
source: Thus, for this target gene, the sma-9 loss-of-function phenotype is epistatic to that of sma-3, indicating that SMA-9 is required for SMA-3 to regulate its expression.
evidence: The manuscript infers epistasis from the double mutant expression pattern matching the sma-9 single mutant.

claim: For five target genes (arrd-19, nspe-7, nspc-16, catp-3, and gdh-1) regulated in opposite directions by SMA-3 and SMA-9, expression in the sma-3; sma-9 double mutant was not significantly different from that in the sma-9 single mutant.
source: Furthermore, for all five genes, as for C54E4.5, expression in the sma-3; sma-9 double mutant was not significantly different from that in the sma-9 single mutant.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from qRT-PCR analysis and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Direct target genes of SMA-3 and SMA-9 shared annotation clusters including fatty acid metabolism, collagens, and one-carbon metabolism.
source: Gene Ontology analysis showed that direct target genes of SMA-3 and SMA-9 shared some annotation clusters, including for fatty acid metabolism, collagens, and one-carbon metabolism (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), but also showed that each regulated its own annotation clusters.
evidence: The manuscript directly states these shared GO terms from analysis and references Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: SMA-3-exclusive direct targets were enriched for ribosome biogenesis factors, mitochondrial proteins, and ER chaperones.
source: SMA-3-exclusive direct targets were enriched for ribosome biogenesis factors, mitochondrial proteins, and ER chaperones (Figure 3d).
evidence: The manuscript directly states these enriched GO terms and references Figure 3d.

claim: Direct targets that were positively yet exclusively regulated by SMA-9 were enriched for genes involved in oxidation-reduction reactions and cytochrome P450s.
source: Direct targets that were positively yet exclusively regulated by SMA-9 were enriched for genes involved in oxidation-reduction reactions and cytochrome P450s (Figure 3e), whereas direct targets that were negatively yet exclusively regulated by SMA-9 were enriched for innate immunity factors (Figure 3f).
evidence: The manuscript directly states these enriched GO terms and references Figure 3e.

claim: Direct targets that were negatively yet exclusively regulated by SMA-9 were enriched for innate immunity factors.
source: Direct targets that were positively yet exclusively regulated by SMA-9 were enriched for genes involved in oxidation-reduction reactions and cytochrome P450s (Figure 3e), whereas direct targets that were negatively yet exclusively regulated by SMA-9 were enriched for innate immunity factors (Figure 3f).
evidence: The manuscript directly states these enriched GO terms and references Figure 3f.

claim: Of nine genes for which mutants were available for body size analysis, only ins-7 showed significantly reduced body size with a Glass' effect size greater than one.
source: Of the remaining six genes for which mutants were available, only ins-7 showed significantly reduced body size with a statistical effect size (Glass' effect size: the difference between the mean of the mutant and the mean for wild-type, divided by the standard deviation of wild-type) greater than one.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this result from body length measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: fat-6 and fat-7 mutants were not significantly different from wild-type in body size.
source: As we previously showed, fat-6 and fat-7 mutants were not significantly different from wild-type in body size (Clark and Savage-Dunn, 2018b).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from body length measurements and cites previous work.

claim: dpy-11 depletion via RNAi resulted in the most severe reduction in body length among the tested target genes.
source: We observed that dpy-11 depletion via RNAi resulted in the most severe reduction in body length among the tested target genes (Figure 5a and c).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from RNAi body length measurements and references Figure 5a and c.

claim: The dpy-11 gene encodes a protein-disulfide reductase involved in cuticle development.
source: The dpy-11 gene encodes a protein-disulfide reductase involved in cuticle development (Ko and Chow, 2003), and the expression of this gene is regulated by SMA-3 but not by SMA-9 (Figure 5b and d).
evidence: The manuscript states the function of dpy-11 and cites previous work (Ko and Chow, 2003).

claim: The expression of dpy-11 is regulated by SMA-3 but not by SMA-9.
source: The dpy-11 gene encodes a protein-disulfide reductase involved in cuticle development (Ko and Chow, 2003), and the expression of this gene is regulated by SMA-3 but not by SMA-9 (Figure 5b and d).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this regulatory relationship from ChIP-seq and RNA-seq analysis and references Figure 5b and d.

claim: rol-6 mRNA levels are reduced in dbl-1 mutants at L2.
source: We previously showed that rol-6 mRNA levels are reduced in dbl-1 mutants at L2 (Madaan et al., 2018), although RNA-seq analysis did not find enough of a statistically significant change in rol-6 to qualify it as a transcriptional target and total levels of protein are also not significantly reduced in mutants (Figure 6f and g).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and cites previous work (Madaan et al., 2018).

claim: Total levels of ROL-6 protein are not significantly reduced in sma-3 or sma-9 mutants.
source: We previously showed that rol-6 mRNA levels are reduced in dbl-1 mutants at L2 (Madaan et al., 2018), although RNA-seq analysis did not find enough of a statistically significant change in rol-6 to qualify it as a transcriptional target and total levels of protein are also not significantly reduced in mutants (Figure 6f and g).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from fluorescence quantification and references Figure 6f and g.

claim: The total cuticular fluorescence of ROL-6::wrmScarlet was reduced in both sma-3 and sma-9 mutants.
source: In L4 animals at high magnification, the total cuticular fluorescence was reduced in both sma-3 and sma-9 mutants, with clear patches of decreased ROL-6::wrmScarlet (Figure 6d and e).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from confocal microscopy and references Figure 6d and e.

claim: ROL-6::wrmScarlet protein accumulates intracellularly in sma-3 and sma-9 mutants compared to wild-type.
source: Interestingly, the hypodermal subcellular distribution of ROL-6::wrmScarlet was altered in sma-3 and sma-9 mutants, with ROL-6::wrmScarlet protein accumulating intracellularly in these mutants (quantified in Figure 6f) compared to wild-type, often underneath the clear patches observed in the cuticular layer, which showed depressed levels of ROL-6::wrmScarlet protein in sma-3 mutants (quantified in Figure 6g).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from confocal microscopy and quantification, referencing Figure 6f and g.

claim: ROL-6 becomes trapped in and accumulates at the hypodermal ER in sma-3 mutants.
source: We used structured illumination super-resolution microscopy to compare an ER marker, VIT2ss::oxGFP::KDEL (Tang et al., 2021), with subcellular ROL-6::wrmScarlet, and we found that ROL-6 becomes trapped in and accumulates at the hypodermal ER in sma-3 mutants (Figure 7a–l).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from super-resolution microscopy and references Figure 7a–l and cites Tang et al., 2021 for the ER marker.

claim: ER structures in sma-3 mutants were thinner, with less complex and branched tubules, relative to wild-type.
source: We also noted that ER structures in sma-3 mutants were thinner, with less complex and branched tubules, relative to wild-type (Figure 7j and l), consistent with a defect in secretion.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from super-resolution microscopy and references Figure 7j and l.

claim: RNAi-mediated depletion of dpy-11 resulted in severe disruption in both intracellular and cuticular deposition of ROL-6::wrmScarlet.
source: Consistent with a role for DPY-11 in the secretion of collagens, including ROL-6, we observed a severe disruption in both intracellular and cuticular deposition of ROL-6::wrmScarlet (Figure 6h; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from RNAi experiments and confocal microscopy, referencing Figure 6h and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tunicamycin-treated ROL-6::wrmScarlet expressing animals showed similar ROL-6::wrmScarlet subcellular distribution as seen in sma-3 and sma-9 mutants.
source: We observed similar ROL-6::wrmScarlet subcellular distribution in tunicamycin-treated ROL-6::wrmScarlet expressing animals as seen in sma-3 and sma-9 mutants (Figure 7m; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from tunicamycin treatment experiments and references Figure 7m and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tunicamycin inhibits the glycan biosynthesis pathway, disrupts ER-mediated secretion, and induces ER stress.
source: Tunicamycin inhibits the glycan biosynthesis pathway, disrupts ER-mediated secretion, and induces ER stress.
evidence: The manuscript states the known effects of tunicamycin based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: RNAi-mediated depletion of genes involved in ER-derived vesicle production and transport (C54H2.5, F41C3.4, Y25C1A.5, and Y113G7A.3) increased ROL-6::wrmScarlet hypodermal intracellular accumulation and left empty patches in the cuticle.
source: Moreover, RNAi-mediated depletion of genes involved in various steps of ER-derived vesicle production and transport, including C54H2.5 (SURF4 ortholog/ER cargo release), F41C3.4 (GOLT1A/b ortholog/ER to Golgi apparatus transport), Y25C1A.5 (COPB-1/COPI coat complex subunit), and Y113G7A.3 (COPII coat complex subunit) increased ROL-6::wrmScarlet hypodermal intracellular accumulation and left empty patches in the cuticle, similar to BMP signaling mutants (Figure 6g; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from RNAi experiments and confocal microscopy, referencing Figure 6g and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nematodes treated with tunicamycin showed a strong decrease in body size.
source: To test whether impaired secretion through the ER alone could compromise body size, we examined nematodes treated with tunicamycin and found that they showed a strong decrease in body size (Figure 7n).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation from tunicamycin treatment experiments and body length measurements, referencing Figure 7n.

claim: DBL-1/BMP signaling promotes body size growth by promoting ER-specific processes involved in collagen maturation, transport, and secretion into the cuticular ECM.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that signaling by DBL-1/BMP signaling promotes body size growth by promoting ER-specific processes involved in collagen maturation, transport, and secretion into the cuticular ECM.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple experimental observations to infer this mechanism.

claim: In C. elegans, a BMP signaling cascade initiated by the ligand DBL-1 plays a major role in body size regulation.
source: In the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, a BMP signaling cascade initiated by the ligand DBL-1 plays a major role in body size regulation (Suzuki et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript states this established fact and cites Suzuki et al., 1999.

claim: DBL-1 signals through type I receptor SMA-6, type II receptor DAF-4, and Smads SMA-2, SMA-3, and SMA-4.
source: DBL-1 signals through type I receptor SMA-6, type II receptor DAF-4, and Smads SMA-2, SMA-3, and SMA-4 (founding members of the Smad family), which act together in the hypodermis to promote body size growth during the earliest larval growth stages (Gumienny and Savage-Dunn, 2013; Yoshida et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript states this established signaling pathway and cites multiple references (Gumienny and Savage-Dunn, 2013; Yoshida et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2002).

claim: There are over 170 cuticular collagen genes in C. elegans.
source: The exact mechanism by which the DBL-1 pathway regulates body size is not fully understood, but is known to involve the regulated synthesis of cuticular collagen, of which there are over 170 genes (Roberts et al., 2010; Liang et al., 2007; Madaan et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript states this fact about the C. elegans genome and cites multiple references (Roberts et al., 2010; Liang et al., 2007; Madaan et al., 2018).

claim: The DBL-1 pathway regulates male tail patterning, mesodermal lineage specification, innate immunity, and lipid metabolism in addition to body size.
source: In addition to body size, the DBL-1 pathway also regulates male tail patterning, mesodermal lineage specification, innate immunity, and lipid metabolism.
evidence: The manuscript states these multiple functions of the DBL-1 pathway based on established knowledge.

claim: SMA-9 is the homolog of Drosophila Schnurri.
source: SMA-9 is the homolog of Drosophila Schnurri, which was identified for its roles in Dpp/BMP signaling (Staehling-Hampton et al., 1995; Grieder et al., 1995; Arora et al., 1995).
evidence: The manuscript states this homology relationship and cites references (Staehling-Hampton et al., 1995; Grieder et al., 1995; Arora et al., 1995).

claim: Three vertebrate Schnurri homologs regulate immunity, adipogenesis, and skeletogenesis.
source: Three vertebrate Schnurri homologs regulate immunity, adipogenesis, and skeletogenesis, acting through both BMP-dependent and BMP-independent mechanisms (Jin et al., 2006; Jones and Glimcher, 2010; Jones et al., 2006; Steinfeld et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript states these functions of vertebrate Schnurri homologs and cites multiple references (Jin et al., 2006; Jones and Glimcher, 2010; Jones et al., 2006; Steinfeld et al., 2016).

claim: At the brinker locus in Drosophila and the Xvent2 locus in Xenopus, binding of an R-Smad and a Co-Smad with a precise 5 bp spacing between binding sites has been shown to recruit Schnurri.
source: At the brinker locus in Drosophila and the Xvent2 locus in Xenopus, binding of an R-Smad and a Co-Smad with a precise 5 bp spacing between binding sites has been shown to recruit Schnurri, which controls the direction of transcriptional regulation (Yao et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript states this established mechanism and cites Yao et al., 2006.

claim: Smads and Schnurri are known to bind DNA as a physical complex.
source: Smads and Schnurri are known to bind DNA as a physical complex (Dai et al., 2000; Müller et al., 2003), but a limitation of the previous work is that only a small number of specific target genes were analyzed.
evidence: The manuscript states this established fact and cites Dai et al., 2000 and Müller et al., 2003.

claim: GFP-tagged transgenes for SMA-3 and SMA-9 are functional, as evidenced by their ability to rescue the mutant phenotypes of respective loss-of-function sma-3 and sma-9 mutants.
source: We generated GFP-tagged transgenes for SMA-3 and SMA-9, and then demonstrated that they are functional, as evidenced by their ability to rescue the mutant phenotypes of respective loss-of-function sma-3 and sma-9 mutants (Foehr et al., 2006; Clark et al., 2018a).
evidence: The manuscript states this validation of the transgenes and cites Foehr et al., 2006 and Clark et al., 2018a.

claim: ChIP-seq analysis was performed at the second larval (L2) stage, a developmental stage at which a Smad reporter is highly active.
source: We provided these constructs to the modENCODE/modERN consortium, which then analyzed genome binding via ChIP-seq at the second larval (L2) stage, a developmental stage at which a Smad reporter is highly active, and both SMA-3 and SMA-9 are first observed to affect body size (Kudron et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript states the developmental stage used for ChIP-seq and cites Kudron et al., 2018 and Tian et al., 2010.

claim: The L2 stage is the earliest point at which one can observe a clear difference in body size for sma-3 and sma-9 mutants.
source: We provided these constructs to the modENCODE/modERN consortium, which then analyzed genome binding via ChIP-seq at the second larval (L2) stage, a developmental stage at which a Smad reporter is highly active, and both SMA-3 and SMA-9 are first observed to affect body size (Kudron et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation about the developmental timing of the body size phenotype and cites Kudron et al., 2018 and Tian et al., 2010.

claim: Previously identified target genes, such as fat-6 and zip-10, were found in the RNA-seq datasets.
source: Previously identified target genes, such as fat-6 and zip-10 (Liang et al., 2007), were also found in these datasets, confirming the effectiveness of the RNA-seq experiments.
evidence: The manuscript states this validation of the RNA-seq approach and cites Liang et al., 2007.

claim: Seventeen genes showed a body size reduction with a statistically significant effect size equal to or greater than one in both wild-type and lon-2 genetic backgrounds.
source: Seventeen genes showed a body reduction with a statistically significant effect size equal to or greater than one in both genetic backgrounds, making them of particular interest.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this result from RNAi body length measurements in two genetic backgrounds.

claim: One-carbon metabolism provides the methyl groups needed to synthesize nucleotides, amino acids, the antioxidant glutathione, creatine, and phospholipids like phosphatidylcholine.
source: This complex set of interlinked metabolic cycles is critical for methionine and folate homeostasis. It also provides the methyl groups needed to synthesize nucleotides, amino acids, the antioxidant glutathione, creatine, and phospholipids like phosphatidylcholine, a fundamental component of membranes (Clare et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript states these functions of one-carbon metabolism and cites Clare et al., 2019.

claim: One-carbon metabolism provides the methyl groups needed to make epigenetic marks on DNA and chromatin.
source: One-carbon metabolism also provides the methyl groups needed to make epigenetic marks on DNA and chromatin.
evidence: The manuscript states this function of one-carbon metabolism based on established knowledge.

claim: The role of collagens in body size and morphology is well documented.
source: The role of collagens in body size and morphology is well documented (Page and Johnstone, 2007; McMahon et al., 2003), and the secreted ADAMTS metalloprotease ADT-2 modifies cuticle collagen organization and regulates body size (Fernando et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript states this established fact and cites Page and Johnstone, 2007 and McMahon et al., 2003.

claim: The secreted ADAMTS metalloprotease ADT-2 modifies cuticle collagen organization and regulates body size.
source: The role of collagens in body size and morphology is well documented (Page and Johnstone, 2007; McMahon et al., 2003), and the secreted ADAMTS metalloprotease ADT-2 modifies cuticle collagen organization and regulates body size (Fernando et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript states this established fact and cites Fernando et al., 2011.

claim: DBL-1 signaling regulates cuticle collagen LON-3 post-transcriptionally.
source: For example, others have also demonstrated that DBL-1 signaling regulates cuticle collagen LON-3 post-transcriptionally (Suzuki et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript states this established fact and cites Suzuki et al., 2002.

claim: TGF-β family members are well-known regulators of collagen deposition and extracellular matrix composition.
source: TGF-β family members are well-known regulators of collagen deposition and extracellular matrix composition, suggesting that this class of transcriptional targets is conserved over evolutionary time (Kim et al., 2018; MacFarlane et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript states this established fact and cites Kim et al., 2018 and MacFarlane et al., 2017.

claim: In humans, there are 33 TGF-β family ligand genes that can be broadly separated into two subfamilies: the TGF-β/Activin subfamily and the BMP subfamily.
source: In humans, there are 33 ligand genes that can be broadly separated into two subfamilies: the TGF-β/Activin subfamily and the BMP subfamily (Massagué, 1998).
evidence: The manuscript states this fact about human TGF-β family ligands and cites Massagué, 1998.

claim: Canonical TGF-β signaling occurs when ligand dimers bind to transmembrane receptors generating a heterotetrameric complex consisting of two type I and two type II serine/threonine kinase receptors.
source: Canonical signaling occurs when ligand dimers bind to transmembrane receptors generating a heterotetrameric complex consisting of two type I and two type II serine/threonine kinase receptors.
evidence: The manuscript states this established mechanism of TGF-β signaling based on scientific knowledge.

claim: Following ligand binding and complex assembly, the constitutively active type II receptor phosphorylates the type I receptor on the GS domain and thereby activates its kinase domain.
source: Following ligand binding and complex assembly, the constitutively active type II receptor phosphorylates the type I receptor on the GS domain and thereby activates its kinase domain (Wrana et al., 1994).
evidence: The manuscript states this established mechanism and cites Wrana et al., 1994.

claim: The activated type I receptor phosphorylates the C-terminus of intracellular receptor-regulated Smads (R-Smads), promoting their heterotrimeric complex formation with co-Smads.
source: The activated type I receptor phosphorylates the C-terminus of intracellular receptor-regulated Smads (R-Smads), promoting their heterotrimeric complex formation with co-Smads.
evidence: The manuscript states this established mechanism of Smad activation based on scientific knowledge.

claim: The heterotrimeric Smad complex accumulates in the nucleus and binds DNA directly to elicit changes in gene expression.
source: The heterotrimeric Smad complex accumulates in the nucleus and binds DNA directly to elicit changes in gene expression (Liu et al., 1995; Wrana et al., 1992; Estevez et al., 1993; Gerstein et al., 2010; Chacko et al., 2004; Souchelnytskyi et al., 1997; Qin et al., 2001; Zhang et al., 1996; Abdollah et al., 1997; Lagna et al., 1996; Nicolás et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript states this established mechanism and cites multiple references.

claim: Co-Smads for all ligands and R-Smads for TGF-β/Activin ligands bind a 4 bp GTCT Smad Binding Element (SBE).
source: Co-Smads for all ligands and R-Smads for TGF-β/Activin ligands bind a 4 bp GTCT Smad Binding Element (SBE); furthermore, R-Smads for BMP ligands associate with GC-rich sequences (GC-SBE) (Kim et al., 1997; Gao et al., 2005; Rushlow et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript states this established DNA binding specificity and cites Kim et al., 1997, Gao et al., 2005, and Rushlow et al., 2001.

claim: R-Smads for BMP ligands associate with GC-rich sequences (GC-SBE).
source: Co-Smads for all ligands and R-Smads for TGF-β/Activin ligands bind a 4 bp GTCT Smad Binding Element (SBE); furthermore, R-Smads for BMP ligands associate with GC-rich sequences (GC-SBE) (Kim et al., 1997; Gao et al., 2005; Rushlow et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript states this established DNA binding specificity and cites Kim et al., 1997, Gao et al., 2005, and Rushlow et al., 2001.

claim: The SBE is considered too degenerate and low affinity to account fully for binding specificity, so transcription factor partners likely contribute to target gene selection.
source: The SBE is considered too degenerate and low affinity to account fully for binding specificity, so transcription factor partners likely contribute to target gene selection (Hill, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript states this interpretation of Smad binding specificity and cites Hill, 2016.

claim: Only a few direct target genes of Smads have been extensively studied, including Drosophila brinker, Xenopus mixer and Xvent2, and the mammalian ATF3 and Id genes.
source: To date, only a few direct target genes of Smads have been extensively studied, including Drosophila brinker (Pyrowolakis et al., 2004); Xenopus mixer (Germain et al., 2000) and Xvent2 (Yao et al., 2006); and the mammalian ATF3 and Id genes (Kang et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript states this fact about the limited number of well-characterized Smad targets and cites multiple references.

claim: In nematodes, body size is constrained by a collagen-rich cuticle, which is secreted by an epidermal layer (the hypodermis) and remodeled over four successive molts during larval growth and then continuously during adulthood.
source: In nematodes, body size is constrained by a collagen-rich cuticle, which is secreted by an epidermal layer (the hypodermis) and remodeled over four successive molts during larval growth and then continuously during adulthood (Lazetic and Fay, 2017; Page and Johnstone, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript states this fact about nematode cuticle biology and cites Lazetic and Fay, 2017 and Page and Johnstone, 2007.

claim: Loss of SMA-9 function can result in a different effect depending on the phenotype, suggesting that this factor can either be an equivalent co-factor, a factor with a more limited role, or an antagonistic factor depending on the specific function.
source: Unlike for the core components of the signaling pathway, however, loss of SMA-9 function can result in a different effect depending on the phenotype, suggesting that this factor can either be an equivalent co-factor, a factor with a more limited role, or an antagonistic factor depending on the specific function (Foehr et al., 2006; Liang et al., 2003; Clark et al., 2018a).
evidence: The manuscript states this interpretation of SMA-9 function and cites Foehr et al., 2006, Liang et al., 2003, and Clark et al., 2018a.

claim: Mutations in sma-9 partially suppress the small body size phenotype of sma-3.
source: Mutations in sma-9 partially suppress the small body size phenotype of sma-3, suggesting some level of antagonism between these factors and challenging the prevailing model for Schnurri function.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from genetic analysis.

claim: The DBL-1 pathway is known to involve the regulated synthesis of cuticular collagen.
source: The exact mechanism by which the DBL-1 pathway regulates body size is not fully understood, but is known to involve the regulated synthesis of cuticular collagen, of which there are over 170 genes (Roberts et al., 2010; Liang et al., 2007; Madaan et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript states this established fact and cites Roberts et al., 2010, Liang et al., 2007, and Madaan et al., 2018.

claim: SMA-3 and SMA-9 have both overlapping and unique target genes.
source: We found that SMA-3 and SMA-9 have both overlapping and unique target genes.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding from the integrated ChIP-seq and RNA-seq analysis.

claim: At a genome-wide scale, SMA-3/Smad acts as a transcriptional activator.
source: At a genome-wide scale, SMA-3/Smad acts as a transcriptional activator, whereas SMA-9/Schnurri direct targets include both activated and repressed genes.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: SMA-9/Schnurri direct targets include both activated and repressed genes.
source: At a genome-wide scale, SMA-3/Smad acts as a transcriptional activator, whereas SMA-9/Schnurri direct targets include both activated and repressed genes.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Functional analysis of target genes revealed a novel role in body size for genes involved in one-carbon metabolism.
source: Functional analysis of target genes revealed a novel role in body size for genes involved in one-carbon metabolism and in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) secretory pathway, including the disulfide reductase dpy-11.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding from the functional analysis of target genes.

claim: Functional analysis of target genes revealed a novel role in body size for genes involved in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) secretory pathway, including the disulfide reductase dpy-11.
source: Functional analysis of target genes revealed a novel role in body size for genes involved in one-carbon metabolism and in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) secretory pathway, including the disulfide reductase dpy-11.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding from the functional analysis of target genes.

claim: Smads and SMA-9/Schnurri have previously unappreciated complex genetic and genomic regulatory interactions that regulate the secretion of extracellular components like collagen into the cuticle to mediate body size regulation.
source: Our findings indicate that Smads and SMA-9/Schnurri have previously unappreciated complex genetic and genomic regulatory interactions that in turn regulate the secretion of extracellular components like collagen into the cuticle to mediate body size regulation.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this conclusion from the combined findings of the study.
